title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
content:
The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply.

About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate.

Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study.

title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
content:
A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.

In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”

Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.

title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
content:
When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning.

The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.

Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”

Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.

title: An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset
content:
For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the ongoing impacts of abortion bans since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of abortion bans has become politicized and federal agencies have been gutted under the Trump administration.

For example, last year my colleagues uncovered a dramatic rise in sepsis rates since Texas instituted its abortion ban, which carries the strictest penalties for healthcare providers. The number of blood transfusions during emergency room visits for first-trimester miscarriage spiked in the state as well. 

Most recently, my colleagues Andrea Suozzo, Sophie Chou, Kavitha Surana and I examined pregnancy-related deaths on a national level. We turned our attention to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The agency collects information from death certificates and publishes totals based on variables like location, demographics and cause of death. It’s a commonly used resource for journalists and academics who want to learn more about trends in mortality.

title: A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon
content:
In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.

The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.

title: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
content:
A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.

Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.

Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, reporting by Drilled and ProPublica has found.

title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
content:
Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.

A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”

“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.

title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
content:
Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the planned departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.

title: If They Call 911 About Domestic Abuse, Will They Be Deported?
content: About a dozen women chitchatted in Spanish between forkfuls of a tres leches cake. They spoke about their hopes and dreams — learning to drive, speaking English, visiting a son who had been deported. Some brought their young children, who scurried around them, circling the tables and tugging at their shirts, before the older kids nudged them into a nearby playroom, giving the women space to talk. The women were from Mexico and Guatemala, the Dominican Republic and El Salvador. Some settled here in west Michigan decades ago and had already become U.S. citizens or permanent residents. Others were more recent arrivals, with pending asylum cases. All of them said they had been abused by their current or former partners. And they had gathered at this informal support group, hosted by a local nonprofit, to talk.

title: Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology?
content:
You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics and grocery aisles: “Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.” “Climate pledge friendly.” Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away.

Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated how the world came to rely so heavily on this premise, particularly in the technology known as carbon capture and storage. CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface, where, ideally, it stays put. The oil industry has long favored the idea. 

At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.

title: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
content:
Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch to bring in more money for policing.

His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the business of immigration enforcement. 

“I won’t say there’s unlimited funding, but there’s quite a bit of money in the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego received $100,000. 

It stands to earn much more. 

Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already received, that’s roughly equivalent to 40% of the town’s $2.1 million police budget last year.

title: Ohio Jobs Program Wants Its Money Back After Company’s Failure to Deliver GMO Salmon
content:
When a biotech company named AquaBounty Technologies announced plans to farm genetically engineered Atlantic salmon at a new plant in Ohio, local and state officials eagerly provided it with incentives. Not long after, the company paused construction and auctioned off “new” and “unused” equipment. Now, the state’s private economic development arm wants its $1 million back.

JobsOhio has requested repayment from AquaBounty by Sunday, according to a company filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The filing also notes that, at the end of September, AquaBounty was down to three employees and $122,255 in cash.

AquaBounty said that its salmon could thrive in indoor freshwater farms and help feed the world. Announced in 2021, the new development in Pioneer, Ohio, was supposed to be its first large-scale production facility.

The project came with promises of 112 new jobs, plus more resources for schools and infrastructure. It was believed to be the largest investment ever in rural Williams County.

But AquaBounty, which had never made a profit over its 30 years in business, faced a tangle of regulatory challenges and pushback from environmentalists.

title: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
content:
When Kelly Joly swiped her electronic benefits transfer card at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, she was trying to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son. Joly had worked for decades as a waitress. The day before her grocery run, she’d received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamp, benefits, she said. But now, her EBT card was being declined. She tried swiping again and began to cry. The cashier told her that this had been happening a lot recently and suggested she report the issue. Joly stepped to the side and called Texas Health and Human Services as her food sat bagged up on the belt. 

The representative at the agency that oversees SNAP in Texas told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds, Joly recalled. Her benefits were gone, likely stolen by fraudsters. Joly said her account showed transactions from the day before at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California.

“I don’t understand why they wouldn’t replace [our food assistance] if they can see that it was fraud,” she said. “And on top of that, how am I going to feed me and my son this month?”

title: The U.S. Paid Insurers Billions to Cover Civilians Harmed in War. Even the Government Says the System Is Ripe for Fraud.
content:
It was supposed to be a safety net for the workers who helped the United States fight its wars — a federal program that provided healthcare and financial support to the employees of government contractors injured or killed in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Instead, a handful of America’s insurance companies have become its biggest beneficiaries. While reaping billions in government payments, they have delayed care for legitimate injuries and received reimbursements for fraudulent claims, a ProPublica investigation found.

Over the past decade, American taxpayers have paid nearly $5 billion to insurers through the obscure program, which the government itself has described as “ripe for potential fraud or, at the very least, gamesmanship for profit,” according to an internal memo ProPublica obtained.

Nobody knows the true amount of misspent money. The official who oversaw the program under the Biden administration estimated that between $100 to $150 million is being wasted annually. The money has poured from a forgotten system for forgotten people who suffered forgotten injuries and deaths in America’s wars.

title: Corpus Christi Started Pumping Groundwater at “Lightning Speed.” Rural Residents Fear the Consequences.
content:
Late in 2024, Corpus Christi, Texas, was desperate for water after years of drought. So city officials hatched a plan to tap millions of gallons of water a day from an aquifer that serves dozens of counties across the Texas Gulf Coast.

The city would drill wells — lots of them. 

Corpus Christi’s drilling frenzy alarmed rural residents, who worried it threatened their access to water. They mobilized to create a groundwater conservation district that would regulate drilling and, they hoped, limit how much water the city could pump. 

Then Corpus Christi officials came up with a peculiar idea. Fearing the residents’ effort could hamper the city’s ambitious plans to tap significant amounts of groundwater, officials asked a local entity to serve as its well regulator. 

The advantages: City Council members appoint that entity’s board of directors, and its staff is made up entirely of city employees.

title: The Trump DOJ Quietly Intervened to Ink a Huge Payout to a Trump Golf Pro
content:
Top Trump administration officials intervened to help a longtime golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley secure a half-million-dollar payout from the IRS. A company connected to Trump’s media business also got a half-million.

The deal grew out of a little-noticed federal class-action lawsuit filed in 2025 by five individuals and companies. The group got $2.5 million after accusing the IRS of failing to protect their tax information.

The law permits a $1,000 payment to victims for each instance of an unauthorized inspection or disclosure of tax data. In this case, however, the government’s monetary settlement is 250 times higher than what the law calls for given the allegations. Victims can receive more money if they show actual damages, but multiple officials say such cases almost never result in payments approaching this size. These generous settlements have raised concerns because IRS Office of Chief Counsel attorneys were not consulted about the settlement terms, as is standard practice, according to people familiar with the case and documents seen by ProPublica.

title: We’re Publishing the Tariff Refunds the Government Has Refused to Disclose
content:
After President Donald Trump’s “emergency” tariffs were overturned by the Supreme Court in February 2026, the government began processing billions in refunds to importers, including many recognizable public companies.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for. ProPublica requested the information, but U.S. Customs and Border Protection denied our requests. (We’re appealing.) 

So our reporters found another way: analyzing the financial disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.

Today, ProPublica published “Cash Back,” a database of figures on refunds for tariffs paid under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The database includes 343 public companies for which we found mentions of refunds, amounting to more than $28 billion recovered or expected.

At least nine companies have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis published earlier this week.

title: These Teachers Were Charged With Sexual Abuse. California Could Have Revoked Their Licenses Earlier but Didn’t.
content:
Five years before police arrested former elementary school counselor David Braff for allegedly sexually abusing students, complaints had already been sent to the state of California: that Braff had sat students on his lap, rubbed their legs and touched them near their vaginas.

But California’s educator licensing agency failed to conduct a thorough investigation after his school district reported Braff to the state in 2019. And the agency allowed Braff to continue working with children. It wasn’t until his 2024 arrest that the agency suspended his credentials. By then, he’d gotten jobs at three more Southern California schools. At one of them, prosecutors allege, another student complained the guidance counselor had touched him, too.

title: Chicago’s City Council Orders Independent Review of Finances as Scrutiny Intensifies
content:
The debate over Chicago’s financial struggles — out in the open as never before — took a new turn on Wednesday as the City Council added to the scrutiny.

The City Council voted 45-5 in a special meeting to give a leading alderperson the authority to hire an outside firm to independently review Chicago’s finances.

It’s unclear if an audit would be complete in time for the City Council to consider its findings before the Dec. 29 deadline mandated by state law to pass a 2027 budget, in what likely will be contentious negotiations with Mayor Brandon Johnson. Later in the day came another sign of distress: S&P Global put the city on credit watch with a warning that the budget wrangling is likely to result in a credit downgrade within 90 days.

The intense council debate over the city’s financial future comes in the wake of a package of stories published Monday by WTTW News and ProPublica that examined how a $55 billion debt burden, decades in the making, was hampering efforts to service Chicagoans and how the Johnson administration was turning to more borrowing to plug holes, such as large police settlements.
